title: Birch porridge spurtle
subtitle: A Scottish stirring stick carved from a birch billet
excerpt: A birch porridge spurtle: 32 cm long, tapered from 22 mm at the shaft to 12 mm at the tip, with a carved thistle-knop at the handle end. Birch shaves cleanly with a sloyd knife and takes a fine knife finish. Food-safe; finished with walnut oil.
sourceNotes: Traditional Scottish kitchen utensil; spurtle carving documented in Lis Paludan, Spoon Carving (Danish originals translated to English) and in Scottish craft tradition from at least the 15th century.

glossaryTerms.definition: A traditional Scottish kitchen stirring stick, 30 to 35 cm long, used for stirring porridge, soups, and stews. Unlike a spoon, it has no bowl; the tapered rod stirs by spinning between the palms.
Freshly felled or recently split wood, still high in moisture content. Carves easily with a sloyd knife and a single, decisive stroke.
A carving stroke where the knife is pushed away from the body with the dominant hand. Used for long, controlled shaping cuts on straight grain.

content.text: : 32 cm long, tapered gently from handle to tip. The knop at the top of the handle is a traditional thistle shape, but a simple rounded knob works equally well for a first spurtle. No bowl to carve: the spurtle is the simplest knife-only project in the spoon-carving tradition.
Sloyd knife: always cut away from the body and away from the hand holding the wood. Never pull the knife toward your thumb; use a chest-lever push cut instead.
Sharp knife is safer than a dull one: a dull edge requires more force and is more likely to slip. Strop before and during each session.
First aid: styptic pencil, gauze, and a clean dressing within reach. Firm pressure on any cut, elevate the hand. A cut that shows fat or will not close with pressure goes to A&E.

Green birch is ideal: pale, fine-grained, food-safe, and soft enough to carve with light strokes. Split a billet roughly 35 cm long and 30 mm square from a branch or small log. Birch from a tree surgeon is usually fresh and carves well. Sycamore or cherry works equally well. Avoid pine and softwoods: they are too resinous for a kitchen utensil.
Draw the profile on the flat face of the billet: the shaft tapers from 22 mm at the handle shoulder to 12 mm at the tip. The knop at the top of the handle is 25 mm square, 25 mm long. Use
s to remove the corners and rough out the round shaft. Work one face at a time. Rotate the billet a quarter turn after every four or five strokes so the shaft stays round rather than faceted.

Start the taper at the handle shoulder and work toward the tip. Each stroke removes a thin shaving; aim for shavings 0.5 to 1 mm thick. The taper should be smooth and even on all four sides. If the shaft is oval in cross-section, identify the high side and take extra strokes there. A finished shaft is round and consistent end to end, with no flat spots.

For a simple rounded knop: undercut the neck where the knop meets the shaft, working carefully around the circumference. Round the top of the knop to a dome with light push-cut strokes. For a thistle: carve four or five shallow flutes into the sides of the knop with the knife tip, angled down from the dome. The stem of the thistle is the neck undercut below the flutes.

Leave the spurtle to dry in a warm room for one week before finishing. Once dry, sand lightly with 240-grit folded paper if there are any rough spots. Apply raw linseed oil: wipe on a thin coat with a cloth, leave twenty minutes, wipe dry. The oil takes two weeks to set hard; keep the spurtle dry and out of use during this time. For immediate use, substitute walnut oil: one coat, dry overnight, food-safe by morning.
Wash by hand and dry immediately. Not dishwasher-safe. Re-oil with walnut oil two or three times a year.

attrs.symptom: The shaft is oval rather than round
attrs.cause: Strokes were concentrated on two opposite faces rather than all four.
attrs.fix: Rotate the billet a quarter turn after every five strokes. The round profile builds from eight equal faces before the corners disappear.

attrs.symptom: The knife is tearing rather than slicing
attrs.cause: The knife is running against the grain, or the edge is dull.
attrs.fix: Reverse the stroke direction and take lighter shavings. Strop the knife on the leather strop, ten strokes per side, before continuing.

attrs.cause: Drying too fast (near a radiator or in direct sun).
attrs.fix: Dry spurtles in a cool room away from direct heat. A light coat of raw linseed oil applied while the wood is still green slows surface drying and prevents checks.
